3. **RateLimitRule** (Priority 3): rate-based blocking at 3000 requests per 5 min per IP.
4. **AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet** (Priority 4): default actions apply (no override).
5. **AWS-AWSManagedRulesBotControlRuleSet** (Priority 5): overridden to Count for the whole group, running TARGETED inspection with ML, scoped to non-static-asset paths.
6. **TokenAbsentChallengeRule** (Priority 6): issues a Challenge when the token-absent label is present — this looks like the critical rule.
7. **BotDetectedHeaderRule** (Priority 7): Count action that inserts a header flagging targeted bot detection.

So the real gatekeeper is the challenge rule triggered by a missing WAF token, meaning a normal browser running the WAF JS SDK would acquire a token and pass through, while anything without that token gets challenged.

Thinking through this further, a non-browser client — a server integration, curl, or SDK — never executes JavaScript, so it never gets the token and every request it sends gets Challenged. That Challenge action returns a 202 with an interstitial HTML/JS body, which to the partner's client looks like a useless empty response: no error is thrown since 202 is a success code, but there's no real payload. This explains why the 4xx dashboard looks flat — the failures are hiding as 202s instead of 4xx errors, and non-browser clients can never pass a JS-based challenge.

Now I want to verify this against the WAF CloudWatch metrics (AWS/WAFV2 namespace) during the incident window, looking specifically at the TokenAbsentChallengeRule's counted/challenged requests and overall challenge action counts to confirm this is actually happening.

I should also pull sampled WAF requests or logs between 18:30-19:00 to see the partner's traffic hitting the Challenge action, and check CloudTrail for an UpdateWebACL event — maybe this rule was recently added or modified right around the incident window, which could explain why the partner integration suddenly started getting challenged.

Also check the ALB-Private origin since /api/* routes there, and pull CloudTrail for changes to the WAF web ACL, IP sets, and CloudFront distribution to see if something was modified around 18:30.

{"type": "finding", "id": "finding-root-cause", "title": "Standing WAF TokenAbsentChallengeRule challenges tokenless non-browser API clients", "description": "The fundamental cause is a design mismatch between the WAF policy and the partner integration pattern. The web ACL example-bot-dev-web-acl has a standing rule TokenAbsentChallengeRule (Priority 6) that issues a Challenge action to any request bearing the label awswaf:managed:token:absent \u2014 i.e. any request without an AWS WAF token. Browsers transparently acquire a token by running the challenge JavaScript; a server-side non-browser client (python-requests) cannot, so it is challenged on 100% of requests and receives an HTTP 202 interstitial it reads as an empty response. This rule pre-existed the incident (CloudTrail confirms no change), so any tokenless client calling /api/* will recur the same symptom until the policy accommodates server-to-server clients. Because 202 is a 2xx, CloudFront 4xx/5xx/TotalError stay flat \u2014 the outage is invisible on error-rate dashboards.", "supporting_observations": ["obs-metrics-correlation", "obs-client-identity", "obs-no-config-change", "obs-no-baseline-traffic"], "related_resources": ["[redacted ARN]", "[redacted ARN]"], "finding_type": "root_cause", "deeplinks": []}

**Why the 4xx graph looks flat:** The WAF `Challenge` action returns HTTP **202**, a 2xx status. It is not an error, so it never registers in CloudFront's `4xxErrorRate` (confirmed flat at 0.0%, with `Requests` matching WAF `ChallengeRequests` in lockstep). The challenge rule is pre-existing standing configuration; the trigger was the net-new non-browser partner traffic, not an infrastructure change. This is a design incompatibility between a token-absent Challenge rule and legitimate server-to-server API clients.

**Ruled out:** `RateLimitRule` (3000/5min not exceeded), `BlockedIPsRule` (no block occurred), Bot Control sub-rules (`CategoryHttpLibrary`/`SignalNonBrowserUserAgent` were COUNT-only, non-terminating), and 5xx/origin errors (TotalErrorRate flat at 0.0%).

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### Flat 4xx graph with empty responses to non-browser client
**Description:** A non-browser client receives empty responses from the CloudFront distribution, with a flat 4xx graph observed. Reported as the triggering symptom for this investigation.
**Time:** 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z

## Findings

### Root Cause: Standing WAF TokenAbsentChallengeRule challenges tokenless non-browser API clients
**Description:** The fundamental cause is a design mismatch between the WAF policy and the partner integration pattern. The web ACL example-bot-dev-web-acl has a standing rule TokenAbsentChallengeRule (Priority 6) that issues a Challenge action to any request bearing the label awswaf:managed:token:absent — i.e. any request without an AWS WAF token. Browsers transparently acquire a token by running the challenge JavaScript; a server-side non-browser client (python-requests) cannot, so it is challenged on 100% of requests and receives an HTTP 202 interstitial it reads as an empty response. This rule pre-existed the incident (CloudTrail confirms no change), so any tokenless client calling /api/* will recur the same symptom until the policy accommodates server-to-server clients. Because 202 is a 2xx, CloudFront 4xx/5xx/TotalError stay flat — the outage is invisible on error-rate dashboards.
**Cascades to:** symptom-empty-4xx

#### Supporting Observations
- **Metrics confirm: Challenge spike with flat CloudFront error rate:** During 18:35–18:55 UTC, AWS/WAFV2 ChallengeRequests for TokenAbsentChallengeRule tracked CloudFront Requests exactly (89, 150, 150, 150, 60 per 5min) — i.e. 100% of requests were challenged. Simultaneously CloudFront 4xxErrorRate, 5xxErrorRate, and TotalErrorRate stayed at 0% throughout. This is the definitive explanation for the 'flat 4xx graph': the WAF Challenge action returns HTTP 202 (a 2xx), so challenged requests never appear as errors on the CloudFront front-door error metrics.
- **Challenged client identified: acme-logistics non-browser integration:** All 599 CHALLENGE records share one identity: clientIp 198.51.100.50 (country US), User-Agent python-requests/2.32.3, header x-partner-id: acme-logistics, Accept application/json, GET over HTTP/1.1. Non-browser TLS fingerprint (JA3 0cce74b0d9b7f8528fb2181588d23793). terminatingRuleId TokenAbsentChallengeRule (599/599), responseCodeSent 202, challengeResponse.failureReason TOKEN_MISSING. Every record carries label awswaf:managed:token:absent plus Bot Control labels bot:name:python_requests / signal:non_browser_user_agent (COUNT-only, non-terminating). Zero records contain any aws-waf-token or any Cookie header — the client is entirely cookieless and never obtained a token. URIs: /api/orders (150), /api/inventory (150), / (150), /api/orders/status (149).
- **CloudTrail: no configuration change triggered the onset:** CloudTrail management-event search across account 012345678901_1 (us-east-1) from 2026-10-08T00:00Z through 2026-10-10T19:30Z found NO write events for the WAF web ACL, its rules, IP sets, managed rule groups, logging config, or the CloudFront distribution. Queried individually: UpdateWebACL, CreateWebACL, UpdateIPSet/CreateIPSet/DeleteIPSet, UpdateRuleGroup, PutManagedRuleSetVersions, PutLoggingConfiguration, Associate/DisassociateWebACL, UpdateDistribution/CreateDistribution — all zero. Only WAF activity in the window was read-only inspection (GetWebACL at 18:59:16, DescribeManagedRuleGroup ~17:45) by a human operator. Conclusion: TokenAbsentChallengeRule and the Challenge action are PRE-EXISTING config; the onset was the partner's new tokenless traffic appearing at 18:37, not a config regression.
- **Partner IP only appears during the incident window:** Baseline (17:00–18:30), recovery (19:00–20:00), and full prior-day scan (2026-10-09 ~22:00 onward) all return ZERO WAF records and zero CloudFront datapoints. The partner IP 198.51.100.50 appears only during 18:37:02–18:56:58Z. This is net-new traffic (a partner integration/batch job coming online), not an allowed-before/challenged-during regression on an existing client.

### Hypothesis: WAF Challenge/CAPTCHA action on non-browser client
**Description:** Distribution EEXAMPLE000002 has web ACL example-bot-dev-web-acl attached. A WAF Challenge action returns HTTP 202 with an empty body to clients that cannot solve the challenge (e.g. non-browser clients), consistent with the reported empty responses. Not yet confirmed against WAF rules or metrics.
**Cascades to:** symptom-empty-4xx

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Add partner acme-logistics source IP 198.51.100.50/32 to the AWS WAF IP set example-bot-dev-allowed-ips, which AllowedIPsRule (Priority 2) evaluates with an Allow action ahead of the Priority 6 TokenAbsentChallengeRule — terminating WAF evaluation before the Challenge rule issues its HTTP 202 interstitial and immediately restoring the partner's legitimate non-browser traffic.

## Reasoning
Partner acme-logistics (python-requests/2.32.3, source IP 198.51.100.50) is a server-side non-browser client that cannot execute the JS challenge, so it never acquires an aws-waf-token cookie and is caught 100% by TokenAbsentChallengeRule (Priority 6), which returns HTTP 202 ('empty responses', invisible to the 4xx graph). CloudTrail confirmed NO config change between 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-10 19:30 UTC — the challenge rule is pre-existing standing config and the partner traffic was net-new, so there is nothing to roll back; this is a forward-looking fix. Adding 198.51.100.50/32 to the allowed-IPs set is the most bounded, lowest-risk option, relying on existing rule precedence (Priority 2 Allow < Priority 6 Challenge).

```
**Purpose:** Save the current IP set definition (expected empty Addresses) to a local file so the exact prior state can be restored on rollback.

```
**Purpose:** Read the current Addresses array and a fresh LockToken; confirm 198.51.100.50/32 is not already present and record the LockToken for the apply step (WAFv2 optimistic concurrency).

**Purpose:** Add 198.51.100.50/32 so AllowedIPsRule (Priority 2) issues an Allow and terminates evaluation before the Priority 6 Challenge rule. Supply the FULL desired Addresses list (existing + the new /32) because update-ip-set replaces the whole set.

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Codify the trusted-partner allowlisting in IaC so it survives redeploys and is reviewable.
**Description:** The TokenAbsentChallengeRule Challenge behavior is pre-existing standing config with nothing to roll back; the manual fix adds 198.51.100.50/32 to example-bot-dev-allowed-ips. Persist this into the IaC/CDK/Terraform that manages the IP set to prevent drift (a redeploy could otherwise remove the manual entry and re-break the partner). Longer term prefer a more durable, identity-based approach than a raw IP: scope down TokenAbsentChallengeRule to exclude trusted partner traffic (e.g. header x-partner-id: acme-logistics, or /api/* server-to-server paths), and/or have the partner adopt the AWS WAF token/SDK integration so their client acquires an aws-waf-token and clears the challenge legitimately.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The example-bot-dev-allowed-ips IP set in IaC includes 198.51.100.50/32 (or the agreed trusted-partner set) so applying IaC does not remove it.
